Hugh Binning
HYOO BIN-ing
proper noun (person)
Scottish theologian and philosopher (1627-1653), author of The Common Principles of the Christian Religion, dead at twenty-six.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

📖 Biblical Definition

Hugh Binning was a Scottish minister of prodigious gifts, a philosopher and theologian who became a professor of philosophy at Glasgow in his teens and a parish minister soon after, yet died of consumption at only twenty-six, leaving behind writings of remarkable maturity and beauty. His works, gathered after his death, include The Common Principles of the Christian Religion (an exposition of the catechism), Fellowship with God (on the first epistle of John), and a moving treatise on Christian love, The Sinner's Sanctuary, and a plea for unity among the divided Scottish church, A Treatise of Christian Love. Binning's writing joins philosophical depth to a warm, contemplative piety, dwelling on the greatness of God, the wonder of communion with Him, and the supremacy of love. That so young a man wrote with such weight and sweetness has made him a marvel to later generations. Binning stands in the dictionary as a youthful genius of Scottish divinity, who in a brief life set forth the knowledge of God and fellowship with Him with rare depth and tenderness, and who pleaded with the divided church to be bound together in Christian love.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Scottish theologian and philosopher (1627-1653), a prodigy dead at twenty-six; author of The Common Principles of the Christian Religion and Fellowship with God, joining philosophical depth to warm piety and a plea for Christian love.

HUGH BINNING, proper noun. Scottish theologian and philosopher (1627-1653).

A prodigy: professor of philosophy at Glasgow in his teens.

Author of The Common Principles of the Christian Religion.

Author of Fellowship with God and A Treatise of Christian Love.

Joined philosophical depth to warm, contemplative piety; died at twenty-six.

📖 Key Scripture

1 John 1:3 — "That which we have seen and heard declare we unto you, that ye also may have fellowship with us: and truly our fellowship is with the Father, and with his Son Jesus Christ."

1 Cor 13:13 — "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity."

John 17:3 — "And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent."

1 John 4:7 — "Beloved, let us love one another: for love is of God; and every one that loveth is born of God, and knoweth God."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Binning's writings honor the recovery of communion with God as the soul's chief good and of Christian love as the bond of the church, against a religion that knows much about God but little of Him, and contends without charity.

expand to see more

Knowledge-without-fellowship correction. It is possible to know much about God yet have little fellowship with Him. Binning's Fellowship with God presses past mere information to communion: the end of the gospel is that we have fellowship with the Father and with His Son (1 John 1:3). The dictionary holds that the knowledge of God is eternal life (John 17:3), not bare data about Him, and commends Binning's tender insistence that the soul was made to know and enjoy God Himself.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the supremacy of Christian love. Grieved by the divisions of the Scottish church, Binning pleaded for love as the bond that should unite the godly, with the apostle's verdict that the greatest of the graces is charity (1 Cor 13:13). The dictionary commends his plea: truth and love are not rivals, and a contending that has lost charity has lost its way. The church is to hold the truth in love, bound together by the love that is of God.
